video.title: Decisions API Full Tutorial for Beginners: How to Use & Set up Decisions API

summary: This is a beginner tutorial for OpenAI’s Decisions API, which returns probabilities for text and image decisions instead of generating a written response. The host demonstrates predicate checks, urgency scores and category choices using hypothetical bakery messages and product photos. The examples show how software could sort and prioritize requests, while routing uncertain cases to a person. The tutorial also promotes the host’s master class, but does not describe a validated standalone business built around these examples.

tactics.name: Test a one-condition predicate and set a consequence-aware threshold
steps: Write the predicate as a clear statement rather than a question.
Test it on one message that clearly matches and another that clearly does not.
Choose a threshold for the action; the host gives 80% as an example for flagging delivery issues.
Use a lower threshold when a person will review the flag and a higher threshold when a mistake could have bigger consequences.

tactics.name: Define urgency levels with descriptions
steps: Create ordered levels from low to high urgency.
Describe what qualifies for each level instead of relying on names alone.
The example uses level zero for items that can wait, level one for replies due today and level two for responses needed now.
Use the returned score and probabilities to prioritize messages, with people reviewing uncertain cases.

tactics.name: Keep routing categories distinct
steps: List the possible customer intents, such as new order, change in order, complaint and general question.
Make each option distinct to reduce overlap.
Inspect the probabilities: a dominant option suggests a clearer classification, while spread probabilities may call for human review.

tactics.name: Add a fallback category and test unexpected images
steps: Define image categories such as bread, pastry, cake and cookie.
Add a something-else option for images that do not fit.
Test both expected products and an unrelated image, as the host does with a croissant, a sourdough loaf and a pizza.
Review probabilities to spot uncertain classifications.

lessons.lesson: Use a probability output when software needs a decision it can act on, rather than generating text that someone must inspect.

quote.text: Instead of asking AI to write something and then digging through the response yourself to find the actually useful part, it just hands your software a probability it can act on immediately.
quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

lessons.lesson: Write predicates as clear statements about one condition, then test them against examples where the condition is both met and not met.

quote.text: predicate prompts should be written as clear statements, not questions, and should focus on one condition at a time.
quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

lessons.lesson: Set action thresholds according to the consequences of a false positive or false negative.

quote.text: The appropriate threshold also depends on what happens afterward.
quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

lessons.lesson: Describe each level in an ordered score so the model has context for what qualifies as urgent.

quote.text: The descriptions are particularly important here because they help the model distinguish between the levels.
quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

lessons.lesson: Keep choice options distinct so probabilities are easier to interpret.

quote.text: one thing to keep in mind when setting up these options is to make them as distinct as possible.
quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

lessons.lesson: Route unclear or low-confidence cases to a person instead of forcing automatic handling.

quote.text: A clear message will usually have one dominant option, while a vague message might have probabilities spread across several categories.
quote.speaker: Mikey No Code

lessons.lesson: Give classifiers an option for inputs that do not fit the known categories.

quote.text: And that last option is particularly important because it gives the model a way to classify images that don't belong in any of our bakery categories
quote.speaker: Mikey No Code
